lessons.title: exchanges complete particles
lessons.summary: Electrons have orbital and spin degrees of freedom. When exchanging two identical electrons, both parts must be exchanged. The complete state of bosons adopts symmetric exchange conditions, and fermions adopt anti-symmetry conditions; local distinguishable spins do not require imposing particle statistical conditions.

sections.title: First determine the single particle degree of freedom
sections.text: Electrons have orbital and spin degrees of freedom. When exchanging two identical electrons, both parts must be exchanged. The complete state of bosons adopts symmetric exchange conditions, and fermions adopt anti-symmetry conditions; local distinguishable spins do not require imposing particle statistical conditions.

sections.title: constructs a combination of spin and orbit
sections.text: The singlet spin part is antisymmetric and the triplet symmetric. The complete electronic wavefunction must be antisymmetric, requiring opposite exchange parities for its two parts.

sections.title: Separating Permissibility from Energy
sections.text: Exchange conditions filter out disallowed states. Which of the remaining states is lower and which is higher requires a specific Hamiltonian; Pauli's principle itself does not give the Hund energy difference.

lessons.title: Find Pauli-forbidden states using projection
lessons.summary: The two-particle exchange operator squares to the identity. Use this to construct symmetric and antisymmetric orthogonal projectors.

sections.title: Exchange twice and return to the original state
sections.text: The two-particle exchange operator squares to the identity. Use this to construct symmetric and antisymmetric orthogonal projectors.

sections.title: Why is the coefficient one half?
sections.text: expands (I−P)²=2(I−P), idempotence requires a non-zero normalization coefficient of 1/2.

sections.title: Zero vector is not a normalization failure
sections.text: The total state of two electrons with the same orbit and spin is symmetrical, and the antisymmetric projection is strictly zero. This is a statistical prohibition, not a numerical error.

lessons.title: S₃, central projectors and Young symmetrization
lessons.summary: Three two-level tensor factors have eight dimensions. The six operations of S₃ produce specific permutation matrices in this space.

sections.title: Actions of the six permutations
sections.text: Three two-level tensor factors have eight dimensions. The six operations of S₃ produce specific permutation matrices in this space.

sections.title: Complete decomposition by central projectors
sections.text: equal-weighted average gives symmetric projection, average with permutation sign gives antisymmetric projection, and the rest are mixed center projections; the three ranks are 4, 0, and 4 in sequence.

sections.title: Young operators differ from orthogonal projectors
sections.text: Choose a tableau with 1,2 in its first row and 3 in the second. Antisymmetrize columns first, then symmetrize rows: Y=(I+P₁₂)(I−P₁₃). Y/3 is idempotent but not Hermitian.

lessons.title: From residual symmetries to order parameter space
lessons.summary: G is the symmetry group of the model, H is a subgroup in which a selected ordered state is maintained; the orbit G/H gives the possible states associated with its symmetry.

sections.title: G and H describe different objects
sections.text: G is the symmetry group of the model, H is a subgroup in which a selected ordered state is maintained; the orbit G/H gives the possible states associated with its symmetry.

sections.title: Discrete points, circles and spheres
sections.text: The two Ising vacua are disconnected; planar XY ordered states form a circle, while three-dimensional unit vectors form a sphere. Different allowed state spaces give different defect classifications.

sections.title: Constraints determine the scope of application of the classification
sections.text: Integer winding of an XY angle requires the order parameter to remain planar and defined along the loop. Allowing out-of-plane motion or a disordered core requires rechecking these conditions.

lessons.title: closed loop, core and winding
lessons.summary: Sum principal-value phase differences between adjacent samples and divide by 2π to obtain winding. Overly large sampling steps can alias large angular changes.

sections.title: Accumulating phase along the closed loop
sections.text: Sum principal-value phase differences between adjacent samples and divide by 2π to obtain winding. Overly large sampling steps can alias large angular changes.

sections.title: Loop cannot pass through the core
sections.text: The angle at the core is not defined. The program simultaneously checks core distance, maximum phase step size, and analytical surrounding charge.

sections.title: Pairwise annihilation requires process conditions
sections.text: The net number of windings surrounding a pair of positive and negative vortices is zero, but there are still two cores in it. A spacing parameter of zero gives a uniform analytic endpoint; sliding this parameter is not a kinetic simulation.

lessons.title: Director, half-turn angle and domain wall
lessons.summary: A planar nematic identifies n and −n as the same state, so θ has period π. This is RP¹, not three-dimensional RP².

sections.title: A planar director identifies opposite directions
sections.text: A planar nematic identifies n and −n as the same state, so θ has period π. This is RP¹, not three-dimensional RP².

sections.title: uses single valued double angle field
sections.text: exp(2iθ) makes one circle along the closed circle, corresponding to the director angle rotation π, that is, Δθ/(2π)=1/2.

sections.title: Topology and energy are separated
sections.text: Topological classification discusses whether continuous deformation can occur under prescribed boundaries and non-singular constraints; stability also requires free energy, size and boundary conditions.

lessons.title: From variable parity to reciprocity relationship
lessons.summary: In a linear, near-steady state framework, L is defined with flows and forces that match entropy production. ε is the time reversal parity corresponding to the thermodynamic state variable.

sections.title: Select conjugate variables first
sections.text: In a linear, near-steady state framework, L is defined with flows and forces that match entropy production. ε is the time reversal parity corresponding to the thermodynamic state variable.

sections.title: Invert odd parameters simultaneously
sections.text: compares Lᵢⱼ(B,M) and εᵢεⱼLⱼᵢ(−B,−M). Here both B and the magnetization M must be inverted.

sections.title: The same magnetic field does not have to be symmetrical
sections.text: The antisymmetric component of the two-dimensional Hall can change sign with B+M, so the matrix can be asymmetric in the non-zero magnetic state and still satisfy reciprocity.

lessons.title: Spatial-symmetry constraints and magnetic-domain reversal
lessons.summary: A fourfold rotation in two dimensions forces the diagonal electrical responses to be equal; the antisymmetric Hall term can remain under this rotation.

sections.title: Rotations constrain spatial components
sections.text: A fourfold rotation in two dimensions forces the diagonal electrical responses to be equal; the antisymmetric Hall term can remain under this rotation.

sections.title: mirror also acts on external parameters
sections.text: An in-plane mirror has determinant −1 and reverses out-of-plane axial Bz,Mz. Check covariance between different magnetic states.

sections.title: Scalar channels cannot misuse spatial matrices
sections.text: Charge-energy are two channels, and the two-dimensional spatial rotation does not directly act on these two channel numbers. The tool applies the selected spatial operation only to the Hall space components.

lessons.title: Dissipation, reciprocity and paired experiments
lessons.summary: Any real matrix can be decomposed into symmetric S and antisymmetric A; XᵀAX=0 under real conjugate force.

sections.title: Decompose symmetric and antisymmetric parts
sections.text: Any real matrix can be decomposed into symmetric S and antisymmetric A; XᵀAX=0 under real conjugate force.

sections.title: Check all stimuli instead of single experiment
sections.text: The entropy production under a certain X is positive, but there is no guarantee that this is the case for all X's. All eigenvalues ​​of S are required to be nonnegative.

sections.title: Let the evidence support the conclusion
sections.text: Save the complete inputs and results of two sets of A and B, explain what is inverted and what is retained, and compare the reciprocal residuals with the minimum dissipative eigenvalues.

cases.title: Two electrons in helium atom: exchange conditions
cases.summary: Combine a common spatial orbital with a spin singlet to explain why two electrons can occupy the same spatial orbital.
cases.assumption: Only exchange conditions for two orbitals × spin are calculated; helium levels and electron correlations are not fitted.

cases.title: dual center orbitals and singlet/triplet states
cases.summary: Compare symmetric and antisymmetric combinations of two local orbitals, connecting exchange symmetry to small Hubbard clusters.
cases.assumption: a and b are orthogonal teaching orbitals. No nonorthogonal orbital integrals or potential-energy surfaces of actual H₂ are used.

cases.title: Permutations of three two-level degrees of freedom
cases.summary: Construct symmetric and mixed-symmetry subspaces, comparing SU(2) coupling with Young symmetrization.
cases.assumption: The tensor factors here can be three local spins; locally distinguishable degrees of freedom do not enforce full Fermi antisymmetry.

cases.title: Vortex model of easy plane magnet
cases.summary: Observe winding of an in-plane direction field and discuss easy-plane constraints and defect cores.
cases.assumption: An analytical XY texture, without fitted exchange, DMI, dipolar or core energies.

cases.title: Director of planar nematic liquid crystal
cases.summary: Compare directed vectors with head–tail-equivalent directors; use a double-angle field to identify half-turn rotations.
cases.assumption: strictly constrains planar RP¹; does not cover three-dimensional RP² defects or actual liquid crystal boundary anchoring.

cases.title: bistable order parameter and domain wall
cases.summary: fixes the different sign boundary, moves domain wall and changes the width, and then uses the domain wall tool to study the specific free energy.
cases.assumption: The real scalar tanh configuration only shows zero-crossing conditions; real ferroelectric or magnetic domains also require multi-component and long-range effects.

cases.title: Hall reciprocity experiment in a magnetic film
cases.summary: Reverse the external magnetic field and magnetic domain separately, tracking the conditions for comparisons with interchanged drive and readout channels.
cases.assumption: Dimensionless 2×2 teaching response; not equal to the complete contact resistance matrix of any four-terminal device.

cases.title: Conjugate variables of Seebeck and Peltier
cases.summary: First unify the conjugate force convention of temperature and electrochemical potential, and then discuss the reciprocity of cross response.
cases.assumption: This page uses scaled entropy conjugates; the matrix elements cannot be treated as experiments S and Π without changing units.

cases.title: One even and one odd variable and dissipation counterexample
cases.summary: operates variable parity, matrix transposition and magnetic state reversal respectively to check allowed response and non-negative dissipation.
cases.assumption: The even and odd variables are abstract near-steady-state variables, not the charge and energy channels, which are both even.
